AND THE VENDORS DISAGREE ON TEMPERATURE: Millipore permits 25 C, SRC-CYTIVA-HF says 20 C 'is not recommended' and prefers 50 C, SRC-CYTIVA-CFF's Table 3.1 prescribes 20 C for a hypochlorite/caustic blend. Cytiva also disclaims transferability of all four variables: 'Optimization of the procedures in terms of chemical concentration, recirculation time, temperature and pH will typically be performed on a case-by-case basis.' WHAT WOULD ANSWER IT: a vendor or published NWP-recovery study on a defined soil at two or more caustic strengths, or Merck's current Rev 7 of the same guide (04/2021), which could not be retrieved - if the chart changed between 2009 and 2021 that is itself an answer.

question: How much water does cleaning this train actually take: what wash volume per circuit, how many washes per campaign, is there an acid wash, and what is the rinse volume?
why_it_matters: Cleaning demand was zero litres in the balance until slice 4 phase 5 and is now a floor rather than an estimate. It sizes UT-WFI, the CIP skid wash tank (U06-CIP) and the aqueous drain, and the rinse is also the medium a carryover limit is measured in, so the gap blocks both the utility and the cleaning validation.
notes: RAISED 2026-09-27 by slice 4 phase 5, as the question the first CIP water figure leaves open. FOUR PARTS, AND EACH MAKES THE PUBLISHED FIGURE LOW. (1) WASH VOLUME IS TRANSFERRED ACROSS A SCALE GAP, not across a molecule: P-CIP-WASH-VOL carries 400 L from SRC-ISPE-WIENCEK-2006, whose 100 circuits average 200 L of hold-up, while our ligation vessel alone is 3,301-13,202 L. Both ends of ENV-019's 250-400 L band are therefore low for us, probably by an order of magnitude. (2) THE CLEANING INTERVAL IS A DETERMINATION NOBODY HAS MADE, and PIC/S says so in terms (SRC-PICS-PI006-3 s7.3.3): 'Generally in case of batch-to-batch production it is not necessary to clean after each batch. However, cleaning intervals and methods should be determined.' P-CIP-WASHES-PER-CAMPAIGN = 1 is a placeholder for that determination and the smallest defensible one. (3) NO ACID WASH IS COUNTED. The same article's facility uses 'a caustic and acid wash for all CIP cycles' at 2 washes per cycle; caustic is the only chemistry this register carries, so registering an acid step would roughly double the figure. (4) NO RINSE IS COUNTED AT ALL, and this is the part with a regulatory hook: PIC/S s7.9.1 requires that limits 'be defined for levels of detergent after cleaning' with 'ideally ... no residues detected', so the caustic itself has to be rinsed out, and SRC-WHO-TRS1019-A3 Appendix 3 s11.6 permits a limit expressed 'in rinse water as ppm', which makes the rinse the sampling medium for P-CARRYOVER-PPM. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: a CIP circuit definition per unit operation with hold-up volumes, a wash and rinse sequence, and a conductivity or TOC rinse endpoint. Until then the balance's cip_water_approx_L is a lower bound and is published as one. See BUF-CIP, BUF-MEMBRANE-CLEAN, Q-074, U06-CIP, UT-WFI, R-008.

question: Are the PIC/S and WHO carryover criteria two independent sources, and does a 10 ppm limit whose stated basis is heavy metals in starting materials apply to an siRNA drug substance at all?
why_it_matters: P-CARRYOVER-PPM and P-CARRYOVER-DOSE-FRAC are the only numeric cleaning acceptance criteria in the whole register. If the two documents are one convention then the criteria are single-sourced, and if the 10 ppm figure is a borrowed heavy-metals limit then it is not a health-based number and cannot be defended as one.
notes: RAISED 2026-09-27 by slice 4 phase 5, with the evidence for both halves already retrieved. ON INDEPENDENCE, and the answer looks like no. SRC-WHO-TRS1019-A3's Appendix 3 states on its own first page that its text 'was previously published as: Appendix 3: Cleaning validation ... 2006 ... (WHO Technical Report Series, No. 937)', and SRC-PICS-PI006-3 records adoption by the PIC/S Committee on 10-11 December 1998 with entry into force as PR 1/99-1 on 01 March 1999. So a 2019 WHO annex reprinting 2006 text and a 2007 PIC/S revision of a 1998 recommendation are not two measurements; they print the same three criteria in nearly the same words, including the shared phrase 'carry-over of product residues should meet defined criteria'. This is the same shape as the membrane cleaning bracket Q-075 holds open: numbers that survive re-publication across bodies and decades are a convention, and citing two documents for one convention overstates the support. ON THE 10 PPM FIGURE'S PROVENANCE, WHO prints it and PIC/S does not: 'no more than 10 ppm of one product will appear in another product (basis for heavy metals in starting materials)'. A heavy-metals impurity limit for starting materials, borrowed as a cleaning criterion. That is why P-HBEL-DS is a different quantity rather than a sharper version of this one, and why carrying both is honest rather than redundant. A THIRD OBSERVATION, MEASURED WHILE READING: PIC/S s7.11.3 introduces 'the most stringent of the following three criteria' and then lists four lettered items, (a) to (d). WHO keeps the same allergen and potent-compound rule outside its list, at Appendix 3 s11.11, so the fourth item is probably not meant to be one of the three - but the PIC/S text as printed says three and shows four. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: the lineage of the three criteria back to its primary source, and a current EMA/PIC/S position on whether they remain acceptable alongside a health-based limit rather than beneath one. See P-CARRYOVER-PPM, P-CARRYOVER-DOSE-FRAC, Q-047, Q-078.

question: Is this a multiproduct facility? The carryover criteria govern what one product leaves for the NEXT one, and this concept has never said whether another product follows.
why_it_matters: Every criterion in P-CARRYOVER-PPM and P-CARRYOVER-DOSE-FRAC is phrased as carryover into 'another product' or 'the following product'. If the train only ever runs campaigns of this one drug substance, those criteria do not bind as written and PIC/S s7.3.3 relaxes batch-to-batch cleaning outright - which changes the cleaning interval, the CIP water in the balance and what cleaning validation has to demonstrate.
notes: RAISED 2026-09-27 by slice 4 phase 5. THE PREMISE NOBODY STATED. Registering the carryover criteria exposed an assumption the whole cleaning argument rests on: SRC-PICS-PI006-3 s7.11.3 limits what 'will appear in the maximum daily dose of the following product' and SRC-WHO-TRS1019-A3 Appendix 3 s11.9 what 'will appear in another product'. Both presuppose a plant where products change over. This register describes campaigns of one drug substance (S1/S2/S3 differ in annual demand, not in product), and nothing in it says whether the equipment is dedicated, shared with other products, or a multiproduct CDMO suite. THE CONSEQUENCES FORK SHARPLY. Dedicated: PIC/S s7.3.3 applies - 'in case of batch-to-batch production it is not necessary to clean after each batch' - the 0.1%-of-dose criterion has no following product to protect, and the residue of concern is this product's own degradants and the caustic (s7.9.1). Multiproduct: all three criteria bind, the most-stringent rule applies (Appendix 3 s11.10), and a maximum allowable carryover needs the next product's batch size and the shared surface area - neither registered. IT IS A SCOPE QUESTION, NOT A DATA GAP, which is why it is worth asking rather than researching: the answer is a decision somebody makes about the facility. See P-CARRYOVER-PPM, P-CARRYOVER-DOSE-FRAC, Q-047, Q-076, R-008, R-015.
